newsitem.title: GERMANY: Prodi meets Kohl for talks amid EMU doubts.
newsitem.headline: Prodi meets Kohl for talks amid EMU doubts.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi arrived in Bonn on Friday for a bilateral summit with Chancellor Helmut Kohl overshadowed by reports of a plan to exclude Italy from the founder members of a single European currency.
Prodi, accompanied by several of his cabinet members including Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, arrived at the chancellery to be greeted by a military guard of honour.
The prime minister, head of a centre-left coalition, has said he plans to tell Kohl that constant reports doubting Italy's fitness for European monetary union are unhelpful.

Britain's Financial Times reported earlier this week that European Union officials and central bankers were discussing a plan which would defer Italian entry into the planned single currency, partly to assuage German fears that the new euro currency would be too soft.

German bankers at last weekend's world economic summit in Davos, Switzerland, raised the prospect of chaos on the financial markets if Italy were among the initial members of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), due to begin in 1999.
Prodi and other European leaders have denied the plan exists but EU officials have told Reuters the idea was being considered by several governments.

In interviews with German newspapers published on Friday, he reiterated Rome's determination to be in the first wave of EMU, saying he would apply "iron discipline" to meet the Maastricht economic criteria countries must fulfill to qualify for EMU.
He cited Germany's commercial banks, its central bank - the Bundesbank, and the British press as the main forces in a campaign against Italian membership.

But the fact that not all Germans are keen to exclude Italy from the EMU starting line-up was underscored by the head of the Confederation of German Industry (BDI), who said he wanted both Italy and Spain to be included as soon as possible.

"I am a convinced supporter of the entry of Italy and of Spain into monetary union and if possible the sooner the better," BDI President Hans-Olaf Henkel told the Italian radio station Radio Populare on Thursday.

"Monetary union without these two countries will not be complete. And for German industry, Italy has a particular importance," said Henkel, speaking for many BDI members who are concerned about losing out in one of their main export markets.
Ciampi, Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini and Italy's defence, environment and transport ministers were all scheduled to hold talks with their German counterparts during the summit.
Kohl and Prodi were slated to hold a news conference in the chancellery at around 1345 GMT.
But Kohl will already be well-versed in Prodi's views from the brace of newspaper interviews landing on the chancellery breakfast table just hours before the Italian leader's arrival.
Prodi told the Handelsblatt business daily he was "certain" Italy would be among the first countries to join EMU. "Italy will belong to the currency union from the start," he said.

He sounded a cautionary note in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, saying Italy's financial markets could come under a wave of speculative attack leading to devaluation and rising inflation if the country did not qualify for EMU.
"We would become a centre of unrest in Europe," he predicted.
